World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Tenants having to fight to fix unliveable, unsafe, unhealthy public housing
World.content:
Dana Wing just wants her family to live in a house that doesn't risk making them sick.

For the past six months, they have been unable to safely use their shower in their Homes Tasmania public housing property due to mould inundation behind the walls.

It's spread to other parts of the house — and there's nothing the family with four children can do about it.

"It makes it hard to try to have baths in the morning of school, especially coming into winter and the colder weather," Ms Wing said.

She notified Homes Tasmania in September last year. Reports were done, insurance staff visited, and the mould was characterised as category two, meaning substantial repairs must be done.

Dana Wing says she's "got nowhere" in trying to get the problem fixed over the past eight months. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Silicone was replaced, only for the mould to come through again.

As the months tick by, Ms Wing says she has no answers, and an offer of a different house was deemed unsuitable for her children.

They are only using the bath, which adds to the stress, while Ms Wing has advice from her doctor to avoid the mould to prevent exacerbating her asthma.

"I've basically got nowhere in the last eight months," she said.

"I understand Homes Tasmania has got a lot of houses out there, and a lot of people to take care of, I understand there's a waiting list.

" Just because it's not visible doesn't mean it doesn't have a side effect on our health. "

The mould behind the walls has spread to other parts of the house, requiring extensive rectification works that are yet to be confirmed. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

A Homes Tasmania spokesperson said delays can occur to significant remediation works if there is no alternative property to relocate tenants.

"When there is an insurance claim involved, this needs to be reviewed and can also cause further delays," they said.

The Wing family are not the only ones in Tasmania who have had to wait for solutions from public and social housing providers.

Years for cockroach infestation solution

Case files for 2025 obtained by the ABC under right to information laws show a range of examples where residents are having to obtain orders from the regulator — the Residential Tenancy Commissioner (RTC) — to have critical housing issues rectified, taking months or even years.

One tenant moved into a public housing complex in mid-2021 and soon noticed a cockroach infestation, their case file shows.

"I called Homes Tas and was told it was up to me to get rid of them so buy some of the bombs for cockroaches … I did this several times and still do now," she wrote.

"I can't afford thousands for a fumigator … I shouldn't have to anyway."

The cockroaches ate through the wiring of the oven, which Homes Tasmania replaced, and then ate through the wiring of the second oven, which Homes Tasmania would not replace.

In addition to a cockroach infestation in the broader complex, the tenant says the property was in extremely poor condition when they moved in. (Supplied)

By late 2024, the residents had set up a makeshift kitchen outside under a tarp, running an extension cord through the window to power a portable stove top.

They had to take the matter to the regulator.

"The cockroach infestation is an issue throughout the whole complex … unless the whole area is fumigated, they will continue to be a problem," the application reads.

"Homes Tasmania continue to refer to their policy that the tenant is responsible for managing this."

The regulator treated it as urgent due to an oven being an essential service, but Homes Tasmania did not respond.

It was ordered to replace the oven and undertake pest control.

These repairs cost Homes Tasmania $2,700.

Tenant blamed for wet carpet caused by pavers

A Homes Tasmania tenant noticed that their lounge room carpet would become wet in heavy rain, a situation that continued for at least 15 months.

The problem persisted despite a minor fix to the roof, so the insurance provider was called in to inspect it.

The tenant was initially blamed for the water ingress, but a report showed it was due to the design of the property, causing further delays. (Supplied)

In its response to a formal complaint by the tenant, Homes Tasmania cited part of the insurer's report that appeared to blame the tenant:

"… the moisture in the carpet was likely caused by nearby plants or [the tenant's] puppy, rather than the roof leak, and subsequently closed the claim."

But the insurers' report had another possible reason, which Homes Tasmania did not mention at that time.

"The pavers outside the sliding door are at the same height as the main internal floor … water could be sponged up from outside and distributed via the slab if there is no damp proof course installed, causing dampness to the carpet via the internal slab.

"This should be investigated."

The tenant had repeatedly raised concerns about the pavers.

Do you know more? Contact Adam Holmes at holmes.adam@abc.net.au.

In ordering Homes Tasmania to fix the problem, the regulator noted that it had not been investigated despite the insurer's report.

"It is not reasonable the tenant should live with carpet described as damaged beyond restoration through no apparent fault of their own," they wrote.

Other repairs to the property were also not completed in time, for which Homes Tasmania "sincerely apologises".

It was also warned by the regulator that further failures to meet repair deadlines could result in compliance action against the state-run public housing provider.

Bathroom unusable

In another case — involving a social housing provider — a new skirting board was installed to conceal mould, rather than rectify it.

In response to the regulator, the provider promised that further repairs would be "guided by its contractor".

The ABC understands that the new repairs are yet to occur, and the tenant has been advised that a full reconstruction is required for the bathroom.

Despite more families sleeping in cars, they're not a priority for housing An analysis of 12 months of urgent housing and homelessness attendances in Tasmania has shown an alarming spike in people with dependent children needing help.

The matter has been ongoing for 15 months, during which time the tenant and their child have had limited access to their bathroom; they are waiting for appropriate relocation.

A social housing provider also did not respond to another tenant's concerns about the state of their back fence, which had resulted in children not being able to use the backyard due to fears of the neighbour's dog.

They also had to take the matter to the regulator, which ordered the provider to carry out repairs.

Regulator a last resort for tenants

These are just the matters that resulted in orders from the Residential Tenancy Commissioner, considered a last resort.

Alex Bomford, from the Tasmanian Tenants' Union, said public and social housing tenants were regularly raising concerns about delays in repairs to substandard housing.

Tasmanian Tenants' Union solicitor Alex Bomford says Homes Tasmania should be setting an example for all housing providers to aspire to, but that this isn't occurring. (ABC News)

Mould is the most common issue, along with pests, leaks and structural issues.

"Homes Tasmania should be a model landlord, so every other housing provider should aspire to reach their standards," Mr Bomford said.

" It shouldn't be the case that Homes Tasmania should be forced to carry out repairs that they're obviously required to do. "

He said there is a tendency in the public, social and private housing sectors to "blame the tenants" for problems in the first instance.

In regard to mould, Homes Tasmania advises tenants that cooking, having a shower, and "breathing" are contributing factors, and that they should open doors and windows to prevent it.

Loading...

Mr Bomford said public and social housing tenants had fewer options.

"If you leave your social housing property, you're back at the end of the list, and you don't have anywhere to go," he said.

Tasmania is the only state where there is no clear process for tenants to seek a rent reduction for when essential services are unavailable, or when parts of their property are uninhabitable.

The state's tenancy laws are currently being reviewed.

Housing stock continues to age

A review of Homes Tasmania, released last year, pointed to the ageing nature of the state's social and public housing as a worsening cost risk, and noted frustrations at property maintenance requests.

The average age of social and public housing in Tasmania is 38 years, and 37 per cent is more than 40 years old.

A new property maintenance contractor panel has been established to attempt to resolve public housing maintenance issues faster. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The government is now in the process of replacing Homes Tasmania after the review pointed out funding uncertainty and policy constraints.

A Homes Tasmania spokesperson said rectifying water damage and completely removing mould is a "complex and time-consuming task".

"If the cause of mould is identified as being due to structural issues or water leaks, Homes Tasmania takes appropriate action to fix any underlying problems," they said.

A new property maintenance contractor panel started in the state's south in July, and will be introduced in the north and north-west this year, in an effort to resolve maintenance issues faster.

World.title: Changes to Queensland train station staffing hours explained
World.content:
Amid ongoing industrial action, another rift has emerged between unions and the Queensland Rail — this time over staffing at south-east Queensland stations.

From Tuesday, some stations will no longer being staffed past 1pm and will be unstaffed on weekends.

While Queensland Rail has defended its rostering, the state's main transport union claims the changes will make commuters less safe, with concerns also raised about the impact on people with disability.

So, what exactly is changing, and which stations will be impacted?

New rostering system

In short, Queensland Rail says it needs to rejig where it allocates staff to support stations experiencing a surge in patronage, as well as imminent additions to the network at Merrimac and Hope Island.

"Changes to our rosters are based on facts and patronage statistics which show that some stations require more staff at certain times, while others are not as busy," Queensland Rail SEQ Executive General Manager, Rob Hill, said.

Staffing is set to change at several stations across south-east Queensland. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

For example, there will be more station staff now at Dinmore Station during peak hours, while Buranda Station will be staffed only between 5am and 1pm, and will be unstaffed on weekends.

"Queensland Rail developed the rosters to ensure station attendance aligns with customer demand and operations, improving efficiencies and supporting job security for our workforce," Mr Hill said.

Which stations are being impacted?

According to data provided to the ABC by the Rail, Tram, and Bus Union (RTBU), roughly one third of south-east Queensland's 153 stations will no longer be staffed on weekends, while 19 won't be staffed after 1pm during the week (previously they were staffed until 7pm).

Queensland Rail declined a request from the ABC to verify all of the union's data, but did confirm rostering changes for a handful of stations.

Station Staffed hours prior to May 4 Changes from May 4 Roma Street First to last service, Mon to Sun No change Milton 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun Removing weekend shifts. Increased staffing during special events Toowong 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun Saturday 0800-1600

Removing the Sunday shift Booval 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat and Sun Removing weekend shifts Springfield 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun 0500 - 1300 weekdays Removing weekend shifts Deagon 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun 0500 - 1300 weekdays Removing weekend shifts Darra 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun Weekdays unchanged Modifying weekend shifts 0800 - 1600 Buranda 0500 - 1900 weekdays 0700 - 1500 Sat/Sun 0500 - 1300 weekdays Removing weekend shifts

Changes at some stations, like Toowong, are minimal while others, such as Springfield, are likely to have a more significant impact on commuters.

Queensland Rail told the ABC new staffing hours for all impacted stations will be available on its website from Tuesday.

What are opponents saying?

The RTBU has labelled the changes "extreme" and said they will make impacted stations less safe. They will also disadvantage commuters who rely on assistance to travel, including people with disabilities, elderly passengers and tourists, it said.

Peter Allen says the removal of station staff would have have consequences for basic human needs. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

"There is innumerable studies which talk about how having somebody at a station provides safety," RTBU Queensland State Secretary, Peter Allen, said.

"For people who might come along to engage in anti-social behaviour, they're less likely to do so if there's somebody at the station."

Mr Allen said the changes would also have consequences for basic human needs.

" No station staff means the toilet gets locked. So what happens when somebody needs to use the toilet? "

Advocates for people with disabilities are also sceptical.

Tim McCallum says the staffing changes would impact people with mobility devices. (ABC News: Charlie McLean)

Tim McCallum, Queensland performing artist and one of the state's most high-profile advocates, regularly takes the train from Springfield — one of the stations facing a six-hour reduction in staffing during the week.

He uses a wheelchair and requires assistance from a train guard or platform station master to board trains.

"[These changes don't just impact] people with mobility devices, it might be people with vision impairment, lots of other disabilities that station staff really assist the community with," Mr McCallum said.

He believed the changes put the onus on people with a disability to let stations know in advance if they were going to be travelling at an unstaffed hour.

" Why should the disability community have to work harder to access public transport like everybody else does? "

Will support be available during unstaffed periods?

Yes, but opponents do not believe they will offset the loss of on-station staff at the impacted train stations.

In addition to the rostering changes, Queensland Rail has doubled its ranks of specialist security officers from 35 to 70.

Some south-east Queensland train stations will now be unstaffed on weekends. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

The so-called 'Authorised Officers', who patrol both stations and trains, are trained in de-escalation and can issue infringement notices.

"[Authorised Officers] work in shifts, which include morning, evening and night times," Queensland Rail SEQ Executive General Manager, Rob Hill, said.

"There is 24-hour security monitoring of the train network through more than 12,000 CCTV cameras, Mobile Security Dog Teams ... and private security officers who conduct targeted patrols of our network."

There will also be a new 10-person mobile customer support team that can respond to incidents during network disruptions or during busy school periods.

Queensland Rail has introduced a new 10-person mobile customer support team. (ABC News: Sarah Richards)

Mr Hill pointed out on-board train guards can lay ramps for passengers who need assistance to board when stations are unstaffed.

But Mr McCallum said this was not a "feasible" solution and would likely drag out the time trains are stopped at stations.

"The train guards, who do a fantastic job, [are] now expected to see a person with a disability down the end of the platform, walk all the way down to the middle of the platform, take a ramp out of the container, fold the ramp out and allow the person with mobility issues onto the train," he said.

"I think that's turning a one-minute job into a five-minute job ... which means trains are going to be delayed for anyone that requires mobility assistance," he said.

A Queensland Rail spokesperson told the ABC it was confident having on-board train guards provide mobility assistance would not impact its operations.

Is this related to the ongoing industrial action?

The rostering changes are not related to tomorrow's escalation in industrial action that will see 273 fewer train services running.

That dispute, around pay and conditions, is ongoing.

Unions launched industrial action over Easter, amid a pay dispute with Queensland Rail. (ABC News: Liz Pickering)

Last week, the RTBU hinted at further rail disruptions after rejecting another pay offer from Queensland Rail.

But Mr Allen said the union is trying to reverse what he called the station "cuts".

"At the moment, we're negotiating six agreements simultaneously," he said.

"One of them ... covers people who are [employed] in stations. It's no surprise we are trying to negotiate an end to the cuts in stations using that process."

World.title: Bondi royal commission to hear from people with experience of 'Jew hatred'
World.content:
Jewish author Michael Gawenda has lost friends and work opportunities because of "Jew hatred".

His experience will help examine the spread of antisemitism in Australia by the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, which will hear members of the Jewish community in public sessions beginning in Sydney this week.

It comes after Commissioner Virginia Bell on Thursday delivered her interim report on the inquiry, making 14 recommendations aimed at improving Australia's counterterrorism capability.

More than 5,700 people have already made submissions to the commission, which was announced the month after 15 people were killed at a Hanukkah event at Archer Park in Bondi on December 14.

Michael Gawenda says he has experienced "Jew hatred" in the community. (Supplied: Michael Gawenda)

In his submission to the inquiry, former editor of The Age, Mr Gawenda, spoke of his experience with antisemitism in the aftermath of the attacks in Israel on October 7, 2023, in which more than 1,200 people were killed by Hamas.

He had been promoting his book My Life as a Jew in Melbourne at the time, and said many of his bookstore events were cancelled.

"Bookshops, it seemed, were keen to have me. But after October 7, these were cancelled, mostly on the basis that staff at the bookshops did not feel safe to have a Jewish book featured this way," he wrote in his submission.

"What I experienced at first was not hatred but a sort of hostility towards Jews that I had never experienced before, certainly not in my professional life.

"I did not get invited to any of the major writers' festivals, not Melbourne, not Sydney and not Adelaide.

"My book had won the major Jewish literary prize in Australia but apparently was not interesting enough or 'appropriate' for these festivals."

'Friendships ended'

More than 3,500 submissions are already before the royal commission. (ABC News: Mary Lloyd)

Mr Gawenda said he also experienced antisemitism in his personal life.

"For me, friendships ended," he said.

"People I mentored did not contact me, not even when the physical attacks on Jews and Jewish institutions were growing, when it was clear that Jew hatred was becoming more pronounced.

"I had lived my life in the public sphere, as an Australian journalist and editor and later as a journalism educator, but I was being reduced to a Zionist supporter of a genocidal Israel."

Closed door hearings flagged

Virginia Bell presents the governor-general with the interim report on the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Hearings will continue until May 15, with further sessions to be held over the next five months.

Commissioner Bell said some hearings may be held behind closed doors to discuss sensitive evidence on matters of intelligence and national security, and material which could prejudice ongoing criminal proceedings.

Antisemitism royal commission delivers first report The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has released its interim report, making 14 recommendations.

Her interim report provided new information about the police presence that was organised for the Chanukah by the Sea event in the days before attendees were attacked, but the commissioner made no findings about whether the number of resources allocated was adequate.

The security arrangements for the event and potential failures by authorities to act upon intelligence information before the attack are among the issues expected to be assessed further in upcoming hearings.

Commissioner Bell can make urgent recommendations at any time, and is due to present her final report by the first anniversary of the terror attack on December 14.

World.title: Emerging Indigenous artists reveal their stories in major showcase
World.content:
For Jabirr Jabirr and Baard woman Ebony Pierik, the decision to learn block printing is about much more than making fabric designs.

"This journey is about reconnecting with my Country and with my culture and with my family," Pierik says.

"I grew up over east and down south away from my Country. I made the decision to move back to Broome so that I could build deeper connections with my family and my community and my Country.

" I think it's been a really healing journey for me getting back into my creative side and re-falling in love with the arts and my creativity. "

Ebony Pierik only started learning to make block prints a year ago. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Pierik is one of four emerging artists from Nagula Jarndu, a women's art centre in Broome, chosen to present their work as part of Revealed, an annual Perth showcase of new and emerging Western Australia Aboriginal artists that draws in work from remote arts centres around the state.

Each of the women has created large-scale silk pieces printed with linocut blocks they have carved by hand, with their own designs.

Their work now hangs in the main gallery of Perth Institute of Contemporary Art (PICA), affording them a major opportunity to be both seen by a wider audience and sell their work.

Pierik's designs are inspired by the land, and her block prints are transferred into glowing repeat designs.

"I draw a lot of inspiration from different patterns that I see in nature when I'm on my Country, like when I'm walking down the beach and I see a shell and I'm like, that would be a really beautiful print," she says.

"One of the prints I have in the exhibition is a Padina algae and that you see this algae everywhere on the reefs when you go out to get oysters off the rocks during oyster season."

Ebony Pierik, pictured here with her designs at PICA, uses art as a connection to Country. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

The swirling shapes have been printed in pink and red on gold silk, a shimmering design that Pierik is keen to develop into clothing one day.

For now, though, she's elated to see it hanging in PICA's main gallery.

"I've never had my art in an exhibition before," Pierik says.

"If you asked me a year ago if my art was ever going to be in a professional legit exhibition, let alone one of the biggest in the state for the year, I would have probably laughed at you.

" This is huge. And to be able to do it with my family members as well, my cousin and my granny is super, super special. "

Aaliyah Richardson has created a block inspired by her family. The design represents a family sitting around a fireplace. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Now in its 18th year, Revealed is curated by Whadjuk, Balladong and Wilman Noongar artist Zali Morgan, who says the exhibition is helping WA garner attention from the rest of Australia

"It's a real opportunity to see the diversity of work that's being produced across Western Australia, whether that be really traditional works that speak to creation stories as well as contemporary responses to climate change and all these different current political aspects as well," she says.

Revealed is a key avenue for launching a career for First Nations artists, some working in very remote communities.

"I think Revealed is really an opportunity that all emerging Aboriginal artists look to," she says.

"Some of these artists are exhibiting for the first time and sometimes seeing their work outside of their house or the art centre for the first time."

For visitors coming to look and buy work, it's an opportunity to see the breadth of work being produced around the state and purchase art, knowing the 100 per cent of the proceeds are going directly to the artists.

The art market has an informal atmosphere where buyers can riffle through the works for sale. (Supplied: Fremantle Arts Centre/Jessica Wyld)

For one day, Revealed also hosts a large-scale art market where thousands of works can be purchased directly from the arts centres and artists themselves.

"Revealed is that moment where you can see traditional styles that we associate with Aboriginal art, such as dot painting or weaving," she said.

" But we also have really contemporary works that really show it's up to the artist what they want to make. Aboriginal art isn't one style. "

Rowena Puertollano with her design, Yingarliawa (Bluebone) and Nganarr (Dugong), block printed by hand on silk. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

For Yawuru Baard woman Rowena Puertollano, Pierik's Granny Ro, making prints on silk is also something she has only taken up in the past two years, and for her, it's all about honouring the stories her mother told her.

"When we were growing up, she always told us stories about where she came from, which was the Baard Country up the [Dampier] peninsula," Puertollano says.

"How various sea creatures, various fish would form the basis of her connection to her Country. So, my design, the Blue Bone, the dugong, are based around stories that she told about how the rocks were formed, how they got their big tooth and things like that.

"I start with sketching. I scribble on a piece of paper and try to come up with an idea on how to tell my mother's story.

"Then I put it on a bigger paper to make sure I've captured what I need to capture. And then it goes onto lino and it's carved out."

This Gurlibil (Turtle) and Jellyfish print reflects a story Rowena Puertollano's mother told her about the marine creatures. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

The Yingarliwa (Blue Bone) is a fish unique to the Kimberley that has a fluorescent blue skeleton that Puertollano has printed alongside a Nganarr (Dugong) on a three-metre panel of blue silk.

On another silk panel Puertollano has printed Gurlibil (turtle) and Jellyfish together, telling the story her mother told her about turtles feeding on jellyfish, and knowing that if she spotted jellyfish, there might be a turtle around too.

She prints on fabric so she can see her mother's stories travel out into the world to be worn proudly.

" You can make it as a dress or something, but it's there, the story is out there. "

All four artists who have travelled from Broome to Perth to represent Nagula Jarndu describe the joy they get from simply working on their projects in the centre, surrounded by other women, sharing their culture and their artistic skills.

"It's a great healing place and it's good to hear the stories when the women are gathering and talking there and the younger ones," Puertollano says.

"I don't count the hours or anything. I look at the outcome, what's come out of it, how do I feel, have I represented my mother properly, have I told her story properly, that sort of thing."

Aaliyah Richardson with the block printing piece she created at Nagula Jarndu. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Like Pierik, she's amazed to find her work hanging in a gallery.

She spent most of her life absorbed in sports and squeezes in time at the arts centre in between working and serving on a number of boards.

"It's gobsmacking — I mean to see my art out there, I've never had the art, my drawings have always been stick people," she says.

"To see it up like that and what I've actually can bring out of myself, it's like, wow, all these years and I didn't even know I could do that."

Revealed is at Perth Institute of Contemporary Arts in Northbridge until June 14.

World.title: Victoria's housing plan will homogenise suburbs, campaigners say
World.content:
A statewide coalition of 21 residents' groups will campaign to oppose the Victorian government's planning reforms, arguing councils and community members should have greater input into how their neighbourhoods are shaped by development.

The Liveable Victoria alliance has been formed in opposition to the state government's controversial activity centres, which rezone land near tram stops and train stations across Melbourne to allow apartment towers as high as up to 20 storeys.

The 60 activity centres are part of a suite of reforms spruiked as the Victorian government's solution to the housing crisis, which also includes a fast-tracked townhouse code and an overhaul of the Planning Act.

The heights of buildings scale down the further they are from the core of an activity centre. ( )

The state government has said the changes will streamline planning approvals processes, allow more houses to be built and help more young people into their own homes in areas they want to live.

"We're doing it because it's the right thing to do and the fair thing to do, particularly for young Victorians," Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny said.

"The status quo was just not working."

Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny insists community consultation has taken place. ( )

But some ratepayers and planning experts argue the government has gone too far, creating a "top-down" approval culture that cuts councils and community out of the conversation.

Jane Oldham is president of Liveable Victoria, which calls itself a statewide alliance of community organisations and individuals "standing up for the liveability of Victoria's cities".

The group has called for the next Victorian government to repeal changes that have excluded councils and community from planning decisions.

"We need to restore democracy, accountability, and community voice," Ms Oldham said.

"This was a promise that has underwritten planning for at least 100 years in Victoria. If it affected you, you had the right to know and you had a right to a voice."

Jane Oldham says Liveable Victoria is not against high-density developments but wants "responsible" planning. ( )

Urban planner Mike Scott, who previously worked for local councils in Victoria and represents independent planning advisory group Charter 29, said the activity centres program was dismantling important safeguards in the state's planning system.

"These activity centre plans are really top-down density plans which have been rushed into place without adequate research or consultation," he said.

"It's not an approach you would expect to find in a healthy democracy.

"What they're doing is to impose a one-size-fits-all model of redevelopment on Melbourne's inner and middle suburban activity centres."

The government has said it plans to build more than 300,000 new homes in activity centres. ( )

Residents call Labor housing plan 'anti-family policy'

James Patto started Fair Growth Thornbury after learning the activity centre plan would allow for the construction of high rises in his suburb and hurt the area's liveability.

"This program is so focused on dwelling numbers — things that sound really great at press conferences — but not actually building good communities, functioning communities that make a place better," he said.

" It needs to be about community building, not just house building. "

James Patto was spurred to take action after the government announced its plan for activity centres. ( )

The activity centre map allows developments of up to 12 storeys on parts of High Street in Thornbury and includes nearby residential streets as an inner catchment where residential buildings can be built up to six storeys.

"I think what we will see over a period of time is the exclusion of families from these activity centres," he said.

"It ultimately is an anti-family policy … and that demographic will change."

There is strong debate over the push for higher density housing across Melbourne. ( )

Ms Oldham said the opposition group was not against high-density developments, but wanted "responsible" planning.

"[We want] reforms that are going to deliver more housing in locations where it's going to be liveable, where we actually consider the infrastructure properly, and we do good, proper planning for housing growth," she said.

Activity centre height limits finalised The government releases its final planning controls for 25 activity centres in Melbourne, with higher heights in parts of Coburg and Brunswick.

Liveable Victoria would provide a "unified voice" to engage with politicians across the political spectrum, run events and information campaigns, and potentially put up some candidates of its own, Ms Oldham said.

"We're providing the opportunity for the individual groups to be communicating what their concerns are about their local areas," she said, adding that many residents felt the government was not listening to them.

Ms Kilkenny said the government did extensive community consultation on its draft activity centre maps, which led to changes based on that feedback.

"We have gone out to community, we've consulted with them, we've engaged with them," she said.

"They were changed based on feedback from residents."

The new controls allow increased height in selected zones around train and tram stops. ( )

Experts call for work with community

Monash University urban planning lecturer Katherine Sundermann cautioned that the activity zone reforms could have unintended outcomes.

"The way the changes are being made aren't necessarily going to get the housing supply outcome the government is wanting to see and are perhaps not likely to create liveable neighbourhoods," she said.

" These changes won't necessarily make houses more affordable. "

Katherine Sundermann has her doubts about the efficacy of the plan. ( )

Ms Sundermann agreed more housing was needed near public transport but had concerns around the Victorian government's approach and the lack of a guarantee of social housing.

"We're seeing individual lots being rezoned for much greater density, but without that consideration of, 'What's the DNA of this place?'" she said.

"There's not that place-based thinking for what a future neighbourhood needs to make it liveable."

Amid zoning changes, long-term residents plan exit Camberwell is one of the first areas to witness the way the Victorian government's new housing development plan is playing out on established neighbourhoods, heritage protections and property prices.

She also shared residents' concerns About the community consultation process, describing it as "not best practice".

"We need community involvement so there's actually social licence for these changes to take place," Ms Sundermann said.

But the Grattan Institute's Matthew Bowes has welcomed the changes as a "really positive step in the right direction".

"What we've seen for a long period of time is that across Australia, but particularly in Melbourne, there are suburbs that have traditionally made it really difficult to build new apartments and townhouses," he said.

"Very few young people have been able to move into them."

The New South Wales and Victorian governments have introduced a range of planning reforms in recent years, including up-zoning land around key transit hubs and in high-demand locations, increasing the height of what can be built in these areas.

Some experts argue planning controls in Melbourne have made developing new housing supply difficult. ( )

Research by the Grattan Institute, which has looked at rezoning schemes in other countries, found rezoning for higher density can increase housing supply and help provide more affordable apartments.

"This will have a substantial impact, in terms of the amount of capacity it unlocks, the amount of places it's possible to build new housing," Mr Bowes said.

"Our modelling shows the Victorian government's reforms will unlock capacity for more than 500,000 homes."

If elected, the Victorian opposition has pledged to scrap the activity centres, expand capital city zones and hand power back to local councils, relying on existing and new council structure plans to deliver housing.

"We will actually build as many if not more homes by having local council input, than what the government is planning," Shadow Housing Minister David Southwick said.

"We think locals should have a say in the planning in their neighbourhood."

More high-density housing would be built around an expanded CBD under the opposition's plan. ( )

But the opposition is yet to announce policies aimed at unlocking more homes or making housing more affordable.

"We need to look at some of the costs when it comes to building and construction. We need to look at tax reform," Mr Southwick said.

"It is arrogant of this government to say we no longer allow people to have a choice or a voice in terms of what's being built in their neighbourhood."

World.title: Tax windfall from Iran war to be pocketed in federal budget
World.content:
The extra tax revenue generated by the Iran war will be saved in its entirety, as the government downplays major cost of living relief in next week's federal budget.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed all upward revisions to revenue will be banked to help pay down federal debt, and savings used to manage growing pressures on the budget from hospitals, defence spending and inflation.

The government is expecting a revenue boon driven by higher inflation and commodity prices in the near-term, with budget analyst Chris Richardson estimating it could tip about $36 billion extra into government coffers over four years.

But the windfall will be used to pay down debt now forecast to reach a trillion dollars next financial year.

And savings measures, in particular a $35 billion belt-tightening on the National Disability Insurance Scheme, will be used to improve deficits that in December totalled $143.2 billion over four years, and offset spending on hospitals and defence already committed earlier this year.

Managing expectations that next week will ease hip pocket pains, the treasurer says the government will be saving more than it spends when it hands down its budget.

"Responsible economic management has been a hallmark of this Albanese government and the May budget will be our most responsible yet," Mr Chalmers said in a statement.

"In this budget you'll see more responsible economic management and more restraint from the Albanese government."

Albanese readies federal budget to favour gen Z and millennial voters Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is preparing to break an election commitment and overhaul property tax perks in this month's budget, to give younger Australians a "fair crack" at owning their own homes.

While the Iran war will lift the government's revenue take, borrowing costs have also risen due to Australia's inflation woes and the Middle East conflict, and the treasurer says "that will hit the budget hard".

Additionally, social security payments tied to inflation are an "unavoidable" spending pressure draining the government's coffers. An extra $9 billion in payments is forecast for the disability support pension, Jobseeker and aged pension, which are all indexed and rising in line with inflation.

It means the government will have little money to play with, despite tax windfalls and the $22 billion in net savings from NDIS reforms, one of the single-largest savings measures this millennia.

And with inflation running too hot, at 4.6 per cent over the 12 months to March and still above target even after accounting for higher fuel prices driven by the war in Iran, the government cannot risk spending measures that could further push up inflation.

Coalition to accuse government of deliberately fuelling inflation

As voter frustrations grow over lingering inflation and expected further lifts to the cash rate, Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson is expected to take the extraordinary step of accusing the government of intentionally fuelling inflation in a speech to the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

"Inflation is not a bug in the economy Labor built, it is a design feature: a deliberate cycle to fuel the inflation, tax the inflation, spend the inflation, to fuel the inflation," Mr Wilson is expected to say.

"We have higher inflation than any of the major advanced economies. It was high and rising before the Iran crisis. And if the Iran conflict ended today it would persist."

Mr Wilson will also say that the average worker has lost about $1,000 in annual purchasing power due to lower real wages since 2022, and $2,000 due to bracket creep, where higher wages lead to an overall higher tax rate, but increased costs ultimately leave workers with less disposable income.

Combined with higher interest payments since the Coalition was last in office, Mr Wilson estimates the average couple with a mortgage of about $736,000 has lost $30,000 in real purchasing power since 2022.

Tim Wilson estimates the average couple with a mortgage has lost about $30,000 in purchasing power since 2022. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Productivity Commission has urged if the government proceeds with a widely expected move to wind back tax perks for capital gains and investment properties, that those revenue windfalls at least should be handed back to workers in the form of income tax relief.

Shadow Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino told Sky News the government had already legislated two small tax cuts due to take effect from July this year and July next year.

The 16 per cent tax rate on income between $18,200 to $45,000 will fall to 15 per cent from July this year, returning an average $43 per week to worker's pockets, and to 14 per cent from July 2027.

"There's a range of measures which we've already put in place, which have benefited people," Mr Mulino said.

"And I think whatever it is that comes in this budget, I think you need to look at in that broader context."

World.title: 'Not being tested': Lead may be contaminating children's clothes
World.content:
How did the leather in your shoes get so soft, or the colour in your shirt so vibrant?

Unfortunately, the answer can easily be treatment with a hazardous substance.

Often, the cheapest way to make a fabric involves treatment with substances like lead.

But in a fast-changing industry with little regulation, it's hard to tell what's happened to your garments while they were being made.

So should we be concerned about contaminants in our clothes — and is there anything we can do to avoid them?

Lead in children's clothing

Kamila Deavers, a chemist at Marian University in the US, first became interested in lead contamination after blood tests showed her young daughter briefly had elevated lead levels.

She began to test items around her home to find possible sources of the toxic metal, including clothing.

Lead and other heavy metals have been widely used as "mordants" in the textile industry: compounds that fix dyes in place, helping them keep colour for longer.

Dr Deavers recently presented a small study to an American Chemical Society conference, where she and her team tested 11 children's shirts from large retail and fast fashion brands for lead.

In their small test, the researchers found that brightly coloured shirts had more lead that was easier for the body to absorb. (Supplied: Cristina Avello and Priscila Espinoza)

Each shirt Dr Deavers tested exceeded the 100 parts per million threshold recommended by the US regulator.

The team also tested how easily the lead in these clothes might leach out of the fabric, finding it could possibly beat recommended exposure levels there too.

Deadly hazards found in Temu products CHOICE purchased and tested 15 toys at random from Temu, with most carrying deadly coin and button battery hazards. Every product failed safety testing against Australian regulations.

"Where children, especially toddlers, chew or gnaw on clothing, the critical factor is how much lead can transfer from the textile into saliva," Dr Deavers says.

She stresses that she used a "highly aggressive" method to extract lead from the clothes and that her findings represent a worst-case scenario.

But her results are not out of sync with larger, peer-reviewed studies, several of which have found heavy metals and other contaminants in clothing.

There's little evidence that these substances are directly causing problems, but they may be increasing the risk of diseases like cancer.

Other contaminants in clothes

Beyond heavy metals for dyeing, a range of other substances are used to make fabrics that could potentially harm their wearers, such as some azo dyes and PFAS for waterproof clothing.

Rayon and viscose fabrics, which are made from reconstituted cellulose from wood pulp, are often made with carbon disulphide, which has been linked to a range of health problems.

This includes "bamboo" fabrics, which have surged in popularity in recent years and are often marketed as safer.

"Perhaps the bamboo plant itself was grown organically, but then there are tonnes of chemicals used to process that into this silky fibre," Rebecca Van Amber, a senior lecturer in fashion and textiles at RMIT University, says.

" If we were looking at the actual fibres that come from bamboo, it would be more like hemp or linen, and we would be making things like rope. "

Softer and more brightly coloured leather usually takes more intense and dangerous processing to make. (Unsplash: Chris Barbalis)

While it's possible that these contaminants may be reaching consumers, they're definitely reaching people who make the textiles.

"Primarily the exposure risk for textiles we know is to the workers," Dr Van Amber says.

Are the substances in our clothes concerning?

Dr Van Amber says she "doesn't want to be an alarmist" about fabric safety, but there is a knowledge gap in Australia.

"Knowing how textiles are processed, and knowing how little they're tested, I think that there's a very reasonable argument that we should be concerned," she says.

"Because ultimately, we don't really know what's in these products. They're not being tested."

In Australia, it's no longer even a requirement to tell consumers what fabric a garment is made of.

Fibre content labels like this are no longer legally required in Australia. (ABC News: Ellen Phiddian)

Fibre content labelling laws lapsed nationally in 2010, and the last individual state laws, in New South Wales, expired in 2019.

Currently, the only labelling requirements for garments are care instructions and some safety requirements for children's clothing.

"Luckily, a lot of brands are still complying with voluntary standards where they're still listing the fibre content in order, but legally they don't have to put anything on there," Dr Van Amber says.

" If all the ingredients in food and cosmetics have to be listed, why not clothing as well? "

In the absence of regulation, there have been a number of voluntary standards adopted by parts of the fashion industry.

The life cycle of your polyester t-shirt We've tracked the life cycle of a polyester top from an oil field, through to when you chuck it in the bin.

These certifications can indicate that clothing has been made more responsibly. Dr Van Amber lists the Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals (ZDHC), OEKO-TEX, and the Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS) as examples of labels to look out for.

But she warns brands can also use greenwashing tactics to imply their clothing is safe. If information on a company's suppliers or environmental certifications is missing from their website, that can be a red flag.

"It really puts a lot of responsibility onto the consumer, and most consumers have not spent their entire life researching and studying textiles," Dr Van Amber says.

She recommends reporting any products you're concerned about to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).

A spokesperson for the ACCC says they take reports of injuries and adverse effects seriously, and encourage consumers to submit concerns through their product safety website.

"Product-specific bans and mandatory standards are made when evidence indicates a high risk of serious injury, illness or death associated with a product," the spokesperson says.

Can we make our clothes safe at home?

Dr Van Amber advises washing any new textiles before their first use — including clothes, sheets, towels, and tablecloths.

"Wash everything that comes into your home before you use it, because we don't know what sort of residual chemicals might be in garments or textiles when they're being produced."

Dr Deavers, who is now investigating the effects of different detergents and washing cycles on lead, says that heavy metals can be difficult to remove.

Enzyme-based "natural" detergents don't have the right chemistry to react with heavy metals and pull them out of clothing, although physical washing can partly remove them.

Older phosphate and borate-based detergents can collect lead, but without thorough rinsing, they can also allow it to build up in scum in the washing machine.

The researchers tested children's clothing from both online fast fashion brands and retail stores. (Unsplash: Zoshua Colah)

Dr Deavers says that washing with an acid, like vinegar, and hot water can help remove metals, but they still can't do it perfectly, or without cross-contaminating the washing system.

"Because of these limitations, post-consumer cleaning is not the most effective long-term solution," Dr Deavers says.

"A more impactful approach would be to address the issue at the source by modifying textile production methods."

Addressing clothing contaminants at the source

Dr Van Amber says there's "too much room" to mislead consumers, and wants to see more oversight and regulation on brands.

There are no overarching laws on textile chemicals in Australia, with responsibilities split between departments and levels of government.

Similarly, the ACCC spokesperson says that chemical management is a shared responsibility between the Commonwealth and states and territories, with the Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme (AICIS) regulating industrial chemicals.

Designers battle fast fashion Regional fashion designers say they offer a more sustainable alternative to fast fashion.

Other international jurisdictions are being more active.

The European Union is extending its Digital Product Passport regulations, which require detailed manufacture and disposal information on all products, to clothing.

Dr Van Amber says this may have a flow-on effect to Australian markets.

"I'm very interested to see how that all shakes out in about one year from now."

World.title: A new poll tells us a lot about One Nation's new-found support
World.content:
Pauline Hanson's sexy new plane, donated by billionaire Gina Rinehart, may have been the political clickbait story of the week, but the bigger yarn baking in the background is that the Coalition's One Nation problem is now existential in the regions, with the minor party not only loved, but loved statistically very hard.

A huge new ANU study out today reports on political and policy attitudes collected in the March 2026 ANUpoll, a survey of 3,662 adult Australians conducted between March 11 and March 26, 2026.

It asks specifically about One Nation for the first time, and the results show that rather than being a flash in the pan, the One Nation freight train may be a lasting phenomenon.

As the nation waits for the first real-time test of One Nation's support in Sussan Ley's former regional seat of Farrer this weekend, the ANU study finds that the rise in One Nation support is not a temporary protest driven by cost-of-living pressures. However, financial stress is a significant factor.

The report says it instead reflects "a potentially more durable and structurally grounded configuration, one where low hope, high financial stress, scepticism about government capacity, indifference to environmental concerns, and a populist orientation toward political life combine to produce a distinctive and internally coherent support base".

Pauline Hanson's new plane may mean the Coalition's One Nation problem is compounded in the regions. (ABC News)

Muted support for major parties

One Nation has always divided the community, with people either strongly for or fiercely against it, but the ANUpoll finds people are not just picking the party to send a message to Canberra; they are actually barracking for One Nation.

Political analysis that matters The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

The Greens top the poll as the most hated party, with 25.6 per cent of respondents reporting a strong dislike of the party compared to One Nation at 24.2 per cent. At the same time, One Nation has the highest proportion of respondents expressing strong approval, with 11.7 per cent assigning a rating of 10.

When it comes to Labor and One Nation, the overall contrast of views is similar for both parties: Labor records 39 per cent with a value above five and One Nation 40.6 per cent, but Labor's support is more muted in intensity. A substantially larger proportion of Labor's supporters express only a mild liking (35.3 per cent with a value between six and nine).

The high standard of deviation for One Nation, larger than for any other party, would appear to reflect a party that polarises, the report concludes. Australians either rate One Nation highly or rate it near zero, with relatively little of the indifference that characterises views toward the National Party in particular. This distribution is consistent with international patterns observed for populist parties.

Populist sentiment is the strongest attitudinal marker of One Nation support. On policy, border control and strict environmental laws emerge as the policy items most distinctively associated with One Nation support, in opposing directions.

Women back the party less than men, but the biggest difference is by education. Those who have not completed Year 12 or a qualification give a much higher rating than the base case (those who have completed Year 12 or have a non-degree qualification).

Those with a degree have a much less favourable view towards One Nation. Counterbalancing this, the employed and those who live outside of inner metropolitan areas have a much more favourable view.

As the federal budget looms, the ANU report shows that Australians broadly support the role of government. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Breaking along education lines

As the federal budget looms, the ANU report shows that Australians broadly support the role of government, with a majority support for government responsibility across 13 domains examined, including health and border control.

But worryingly for the government, the belief-in-government index declined between December 2025 and March 2026, consistent with falling institutional confidence over this period.

Albanese's second term was rewritten by events One year ago, Anthony Albanese was a man on top of the world.

Attitudes to the budget also reflect a well-documented paradox: support for spending to stimulate the economy is down, concern about public debt has reached a peak level, and more Australians than ever believe their income taxes are too high, yet majorities still want more government spending across most budget areas.

Imagine designing a budget with these contradictory messages coming at you.

Environmental attitudes show a modest shift under conditions of economic strain. The proportion of Australians believing the country does too little for the environment has declined from pandemic-era levels, though it remains the most common view.

Nearly three in 10 Australians rate global warming as not serious or not very serious, a higher scepticism rate than for any other environmental issue asked about.

Debt is a big concern, with 30 per cent of people very worried about government debt, higher than in any previous ANUpoll series. When you combine this number with those saying they are somewhat worried, that cohort represents three-quarters of the population (75.6 per cent).

So we seem to have a population that is financially squeezed, has diminished confidence in government's ability to deliver, and is at the same time unwilling to accept either taxes that more spending would require or debt that would otherwise fund it.

This may be contradictory, but it is a contradiction that the Albanese government must handle now, and that project is only getting harder as politics realigns.

Loading

Patricia Karvelas is the host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

World.title: Suaalii’s dream Twickenham debut is a millstone around his neck
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionSuper Rugby Suaalii’s dream Twickenham debut is a millstone around his neck Paul Cully May 4, 2026 — 5:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii’s muted return against the Western Force in Sydney on Friday night was partly due to the visitors’ smart tactics of starving the Waratahs of the ball. It was further evidence of how adept Australian teams are at shutting each other down. Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii (centre) made a quiet return for the Waratahs against the Western Force on Friday night. Getty Images It was also because he missed more than a month of rugby due to a hamstring injury, and his timing isn’t quite in sync with his teammates. But the third part of this narrative is that the quality of Suaalii’s debut performance against England at the end of 2024 was inflated far above reality.



It has set an expectation that he will dominate every contest, and no other No.13 in the world is doing that. That Twickenham Test against England, won 42-37 by the Wallabies, has been like a millstone around his neck ever since, though it’s clear he is still very much in the learning stage of his rugby career. The Waratahs’ Lawson Creighton did a great job of negating Zac Lomax’s impact in the air. Getty Images But don’t be surprised if he is much more influential against the Highlanders in Dunedin next Saturday afternoon. The Force’s ability to limit Suaalii’s impact was mirrored by how cleverly the Waratahs limited Zac Lomax’s influence under the high ball and reflected a bigger picture: the four Australian teams have been each other’s worst enemies in Super Rugby. Look at the ladder: despite the Brumbies having a 4-1 record against the Kiwis and the Reds are 2-2 in trans-Tasman games ahead of their clash with the Chiefs on Friday, the Reds are fourth, the Brumbies are sixth, the Waratahs are eighth and the Force are 10th.



So, the Waratahs’ use of Lawson Creighton to contest the high ball against Lomax was just the latest sign of how adept Australian teams have become at negating each other. The Waratahs have beaten the Brumbies and Reds, while the Queenslanders have swept the Brumbies but lost at home to the Force – and on it goes. Equality is hurting Australia The supreme irony of the dilemma described above is that an equal distribution of talent – what should be a force for good – is actually hurting Australia’s hopes of securing a home play-off. Man for man, the Australian squads are relatively even compared to the situation in New Zealand, where the weakest side – the Highlanders – is a level below the other four. The other four Kiwi sides have beaten the Highlanders so far, and the Hurricanes and Chiefs are odds-on to defeat them twice before the end of the regular season. Advocates for a trans-Tasman player draft are on the right track but are overreaching.



Australia should tell New Zealand they need to replicate the talent spread present in their own system, where the form Australian No.9, No.10 and outside back are all in Perth (see item below). Failing that, Rugby Australia should push hard for a conference system in a 10-team competition next year, where the top two sides in Australia make the semi-finals. Super Rugby team of the week 1. Sef Fa’agaese (Force), 2. Brandon Paenga-Amosa (Force), 3. Zane Nonggorr (Reds), 4. Seru Uru (Reds), 5. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto (Reds), 6. Joe Brial (Reds), 7. Fraser McReight (Reds), 8. Nick Champion de Crespigny (Force), 9. Henry Robertson (Force), 10. Ben Donaldson (Force) - player of the week, 11. Dylan Pietsch (Force), 12. Hunter Paisami (Reds), 13. Josh Flook (Reds), 14. Filipo Daugunu (Reds), 15. Mac Grealy (Force) Good signs for Joe Schmidt The Reds-Brumbies game in Brisbane was the best match of the weekend. It was intense, but punctuated by moments of individual skill: Joe Brial’s pick up down the right-hand touchline and Jock Campbell’s big touch finder off his left boot among them.



As the July Tests approach, it was a reassuring sight for Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt. The Leinster contingent in first-up opponents Ireland again showed their quality over the weekend by beating Toulon to qualify for the Champions Cup final, so the Wallabies will need to hit the ground running. Big Lukhan Salakaia-Loto is in great form, Hunter Paisami was nice and direct, and the Reds’ back row of Brial, Fraser McReight and Harry Wilson pipped their opposites. The Robertson, Donaldson show Force No.10 Ben Donaldson is in career-best form, but it is almost impossible to separate his excellent performance against the Waratahs from the quality of his halves partner Henry Robertson. The Force No.9 will make his Wallabies debut this year – you can put your house on it. Related Article Waratahs ‘We were bullied’: Waratahs take a beating from Force in Sydney



No other halfback in Australia has linked his forwards and backs as well as Robertson during the past month or so, and his running threat around the ruck creates space for Donaldson. His box-kicking is also outstanding. As mentioned in item one, only the strength of Waratahs No.10 Creighton under the high ball in Sydney prevented Lomax from having a field day. But not even Creighton could stop Dylan Pietsch, the Force winger who is now setting the standard for Australian outside backs. Watch every match of Super Rugby Pacific live and exclusive on Stan Sport.

World.title: ASX set to slip, Wall Street sets more records
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip, Wall Street sets more records Stan Choe May 4, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market set more records after Apple, Estee Lauder and others joined the list of companies delivering fatter profits for the start of the year than analysts expected. Easing oil prices also helped steady the stock markets around the world that were still open on the May Day holiday. The S&P 500 climbed 0.3 per cent to its latest all-time high and closed out a fifth straight winning week. That’s its longest such streak since 2024. The Dow Jones dipped 152 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.9 per cent to its own record. Wall Street continues to rise despite the uncertainty of the Iran war. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures on Saturday pointing to a fall of 23 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.99¢ at 5.15am AEST. Front of mind for investors this week will be the Reserve Bank’s interest rates decision on Tuesday afternoon. Apple led the way on Wall Street after the iPhone seller reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Because it’s one of Wall Street’s biggest stocks in terms of overall size, Apple’s rally of 3.3 per cent was by far the strongest force lifting the S&P 500.



Stock prices generally follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, and US companies have been blowing past expectations for earnings in the first three months of 2026. That’s even with the war with Iran and high oil prices souring confidence for many US households. A little more than a quarter of the companies in the S&P 500 have reported already, and 84 per cent of them have topped analysts’ estimates, according to FactSet. The index is on track to deliver roughly 15 per cent growth in profit from a year earlier. Related Article Opinion

Cybersecurity The AI craze is a double-edged sword for our banking giants Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Estee Lauder’s stock climbed 3.4 per cent after reporting better earnings than expected, thanks in part to strength in China, and it raised some of its upcoming financial forecasts. Sandisk jumped 8.3 per cent after the maker of storage for computers blew past analysts’ expectations for profit thanks in part to voracious demand from data centres. Colgate-Palmolive added 2.2 per cent after likewise delivering bigger results than expected, though CEO Noel Wallace said it expects “volatile macroeconomic conditions and slower category growth to continue in 2026.”



The main uncertainty for the global economy is where oil prices are heading because of the Iran war. Oil prices spurted higher early this week on worries that the war will keep the Strait of Hormuz closed for a long time. That would in turn keep oil tankers pent up in the Persian Gulf instead of delivering crude to customers worldwide. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s war has been a gift to an industry he detests But such moves have been quick to reverse throughout the war, as hopes rise and fall for a reopening of the strait. On Friday, the price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 2 per cent to settle at $US108.17. Brent was selling for a little more than $US70 per barrel before the war began. That rise since the end of February helped the two biggest US oil companies report stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. But stock prices nevertheless fell for both Exxon Mobil, 1 per cent, and Chevron, 1.4 per cent, as oil prices regressed Friday and each reported drops in net income from a year earlier. All told, the S&P 500 rose 21.11 points to 7,230.12. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 152.87 to 49,499.27, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 222.13 to 25,114.44.



The fall in oil prices helped Treasury yields ease in the bond market. So did a report in the morning that said growth for US manufacturing was a touch softer last month than economists expected. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.38 per cent from 4.40 per cent late Thursday. Such dips can make mortgages and other loans for US households and businesses cheaper, and they also tend to give upward pushes to prices for stocks and all kinds of other investments. Many stock markets worldwide were closed for May Day. Among the indexes still trading, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.4 per cent, and London’s FTSE 100 slipped 0.1 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Antonelli wins Miami Grand Prix as Oscar Piastri finishes third
World.content:
Breaking SportFormula 1 Antonelli wins Miami Grand Prix as Oscar Piastri finishes third Field Level Media May 4, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami, Florida: Kimi Antonelli won the Miami Grand Prix on Sunday for his third consecutive Formula 1 victory as the 19-year-old Mercedes driver continued to show he’s a legitimate championship contender. Antonelli started from the pole but had a slick start on a damp surface at the Miami International Autodrome. Threats of heavy rain led F1 to move up the start of the race by three hours, and there was an early morning heavy thunderstorm with lightning strikes directly over the Hard Rock Stadium, but it had cleared by the time the event began. Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli of Italy celebrates after winning the Miami Formula One Grand Prix. AP Still, the first 25 laps were attacked by the drivers as if the rain could return at any moment, and it led to early chaos, even for Antonelli. Charles Leclerc of Ferrari had a spectacular start from third and surged to the lead when Antonelli went wide off course trying to defend. A split-second later, Max Verstappen spun trying to hold off Leclerc when the two cars made contact.



The contact caused Verstappen, who started a season-best second, to plummet to ninth after the spin. Antonelli recovered and reclaimed the lead on the fifth lap, and the leaders briefly swapped positions as Leclerc moved back to the front before reigning world champion Lando Norris took over on Lap 14. Oscar Piastri before the race. Getty Images Verstappen worked his way through the field and briefly took the lead as others pitted, but Antonelli beat Norris off pit lane and reclaimed the lead for good once everything cycled out. Norris finished second, 3.2 seconds behind Antonelli, as the Italian and teammate George Russell have won the first four races of this season for Mercedes. Leclerc was going to finish third until Oscar Piastri of McLaren passed him on the final lap. Leclerc spun and settled for sixth.



Russell was fourth and Verstappen finished a season-best fifth for Red Bull. Lewis Hamilton of Ferrari was seventh. Oscar Piastri overtook Charles Leclerc to finish third. Getty Images Cadillac, in its first race in the United States, had an unimpressive weekend on the track even as it splashed its way through Miami with appearances and events. Sergio Perez finished 16th and Valtteri Bottas was 18th — the last car to finish in the 22-driver field. Messy start Isack Hadjar had been disqualified after qualifying and started last, but his race lasted five laps before he drove his Red Bull into the wall. Hadjar was openly angry at the result as he pounded his helmet before climbing from his car and angrily stomping away.



Seconds later, Pierre Gasly and Liam Lawson made contact that caused Gasly’s car to do a full rollover. The Frenchman’s car ended stuck with its rear tires atop a barrier and he climbed from the half-suspended BMW on his own. Up next The Canadian Grand Prix is next for F1 at Circuit Gilles Villeneuve in Montreal on May 24. That date was traditionally held by the Monaco Grand Prix but a tweak to the schedule shifted it to Canada, and F1 will no longer be the opener for what had traditionally been the most prolific day in motorsports. The F1 race typically opened the morning ahead of the Indianapolis 500 and then NASCAR’s Coca-Cola 600. Because the race is in Canada and not Monaco, it has a late afternoon start time and will follow the Indy 500 and end during the NASCAR race. AP
